claims.text: Adding a controlled low-volume fraction of nanoscale Y2O3 dispersoids will enhance the mechanical performance of refractory high-entropy alloys under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The baseline alloy has a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure.
The baseline alloy lacks intentional oxide dispersions.
The proposed processing intervention can produce a uniform nanoscale Y2O3 dispersion.
The Y2O3 dispersoids will remain stable and uniformly distributed under the stated conditions.
Nanoscale Y2O3 dispersoids act as pinning centers for dislocations.
Nanoscale Y2O3 dispersoids act as pinning or trapping centers for irradiation-induced defect clusters.
The dispersoids trap or promote recombination of irradiation-induced point defects.
Impeded dislocation motion strengthens the alloy.
Defect trapping or recombination helps maintain irradiation stability.
The modified alloy will have greater yield strength than the oxide-free baseline under combined high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The modified alloy will have greater ductility than the oxide-free baseline under combined high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The modified alloy will accumulate fewer irradiation-induced defects than the oxide-free baseline.
The anticipated benefits require a uniform and optimal dispersoid distribution.
An excessive Y2O3 volume fraction or non-uniform dispersion may cause embrittlement.
An excessive Y2O3 volume fraction or non-uniform dispersion may impair thermal stability.

contradictions.description: The stated benefit is conditional on uniform, optimal dispersion, but the experiment treats non-uniform dispersion as falsification. Non-uniform dispersion instead violates the hypothesis's stated applicability condition and could indicate unsuccessful processing rather than falsify the proposed mechanism.
